title: Gargi's questions in Janaka's court
hook: a king pays for an argument, and a woman asks the hardest questions in the room
carry: reasoned inquiry is the lamp of all learning
tomorrow: the whole science, it says, is one victory. over whom?

segments.voice: Yesterday, before you begin, bow to your teachers: Kacha in the enemy's house, and the Arthashastra's bow to both sides. Today, the arguing starts.

King Janaka of Videha holds a great sacrifice and sets out a prize: a thousand cows with gold tied to their horns, for the most learned person in the room. The sage Yajnavalkya simply tells his student to drive the cows home. Uproar. The scholars line up to test him, one after another. Then Gargi Vachaknavi stands. She asks what everything is woven on, then what that is woven on, and keeps pushing, until Yajnavalkya warns her: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. She sits. Later she stands again, asks the assembly's leave, and fires two more questions, like arrows.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS FOR THE WISEST.` → `GARGI KEEPS ASKING.` → `SHE COMES BACK WITH TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and look at what it keeps. A king's court that pays for argument. A woman who presses the greatest sage in the land, and comes back for more. When she's done, she tells the scholars plainly that none of them will beat him in debate about Brahman. Hindu tradition has a name for formal argument over the texts, shastrartha, and it never stopped: schools answer schools, and many teachers take a sharp question as respect. The Arthashastra, this week's handbook on power, builds that respect into a ruler's training. It names four sciences: anvikshiki, reasoned inquiry; the Vedas; varta, farming, cattle and trade; and dandaniti, government. It even lets rival schools speak first: one counts three sciences, one two, and one only government, because every other learning depends on order. Then it keeps all four and crowns reasoned inquiry, in paraphrase, the lamp of all sciences, the means of all action, the support of all dharma. It keeps the mind steady in good times and bad. That's the teaching. In this tradition, asking is part of the faith, not a threat to it, and a king who wants to rule well puts questions at the center of his court.
screen: `A COURT THAT PAYS FOR ARGUMENT.` · `SHASTRARTHA: DEBATE OVER THE TEXTS.` · `FOUR SCIENCES FOR A RULER.` · `RIVALS FIRST, THEN ANVIKSHIKI: THE LAMP OF ALL SCIENCES.` · then, large: `ASKING IS PART OF THE FAITH.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu study sessions open with an old peace prayer, saha navavatu: may we be protected together, may our learning shine, may we never quarrel. If you pray, say it, or its meaning, quietly. If you don't, bring to mind one question you've been afraid to ask, and hold it gently while you breathe.
The Arthashastra's opening: anvikshiki, reasoned inquiry, which it calls the lamp of all the sciences.
For the road: reasoned inquiry is the lamp of all learning. Gargi held it up in a king's court. Day fifteen eighty-five.

howItsDone: Hindu scholars and schools still hold shastrartha, formal debate over the texts, and many study sessions open with the peace prayer saha navavatu, asking that teacher and student learn together without quarrel.

fork.setup: at temple youth class you ask why we offer food to the gods before we eat it. an aunty says 'don't question.' by Gargi's story, what's the hindu way?
options: ask, with respect. questions sit at the heart of the tradition.

fork.reveal: Gargi asked, sat when warned, and came back with the assembly's leave. the Upanishads are full of questions, and the Arthashastra calls reasoned inquiry the lamp. asking, with respect, is the tradition.

Janaka.meaning: king of Videha, famed for his learned court

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage tested in Janaka's court

Gargi Vachaknavi.meaning: the woman philosopher who questioned Yajnavalkya

shastrartha.meaning: formal debate over the meaning of texts

anvikshiki.meaning: reasoned inquiry, examining things before acting

varta.meaning: the science of farming, cattle and trade

saha navavatu.meaning: a peace prayer said before study: may we be protected together

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1 (Janaka's prize of a thousand cows; Yajnavalkya has them driven home), 3.6 (Gargi's first questions and the warning), 3.8 (Gargi's two questions 'like arrows'; she tells the brahmins none will defeat him)
Arthashastra 1.2 (the sciences: anvikshiki, trayi, varta, dandaniti; the counts of the schools of Manu, Brihaspati and Ushanas; anvikshiki as the lamp of all sciences)

notes: Arthashastra run, day 2. The counts (four; Manu's school three; Brihaspati's two; Ushanas's one) are the text's own (1.2). Confirm.
The one-science school's reason (all other sciences depend on government) paraphrases 1.2; confirm. Brihaspati's school's stated reason (the Vedas as a cover) is left out on purpose.
Ushanas as another name for Shukra: standard; confirm. The voice links it to yesterday's salutation.

'The lamp of all sciences, the means of all action, the support of all dharma' paraphrases 1.2.12; 'steady in good times and bad … skilled in thinking, speaking and acting' paraphrases 1.2.11. Not quoted: no listed public-domain translation.
